l: Surah 76: Man (Al-Insaan), Surah 76: Man (Al-Insaan), Surah 76: Man (Al-Insaan)
s: Surah 76: Man (Al-Insaan) concerns man, his creation, guidance, choices, and ultimate consequences. Allah creates man from a drop of thickened fluid, shows him the way, and prepares differing outcomes for the grateful, the righteous, and the disbelievers. The righteous receive a Garden, fine clothing, pure drink, and acceptance of their endeavour, while disbelievers and evil-doers face punishment. The unit also concerns the Qur'an as a revelation and instructs submission, remembrance, and worship of Allah.

l: Surah 76: Man (Al-Insaan), Surah 76: Man (Al-Insaan), Surah 76: Man (Al-Insaan)
s: Surah 76: Man (Al-Insaan) describes man's creation, guidance, duties, and final outcomes. It presents Allah's rewards for the righteous and punishment for disbelievers and evil-doers.
Man is created from a drop of thickened fluid and is made hearing and knowing. Man is shown the way and may be grateful or disbelieving; Allah can replace people with others like them.

Allah creates man, shows him the way, prepares manacles, carcans, and a raging fire for disbelievers, and wards evil away from the righteous. Allah rewards those who endure, reveals the Qur'an, is Knower and Wise, and admits whom He wills into His mercy.

l: the righteous, Surah 76: Man (Al-Insaan), Surah 76: Man (Al-Insaan)
s: The righteous drink from cups mixed with Kafur and Zanjabil and feed the needy, the orphan, and the prisoner for the sake of Allah. Allah wards the evil of the day from them and awards them a Garden, silk attire, joy, and pure drink.
Disbelievers have manacles, carcans, and a raging fire prepared for them. They are also among those whose conduct is opposed by the command to obey Allah rather than any guilty one or disbeliever.

l: the Qur'an, Surah 76: Man (Al-Insaan), Surah 76: Man (Al-Insaan)
s: The Qur'an is revealed by Allah as a revelation. The unit instructs the addressed person to submit patiently to Allah's command.
Revelation is identified with Allah's revealing the Qur'an. It is presented as an admonishment through which whoever wills may choose a way unto his Lord.
The Garden is awarded to the righteous for all that they endured. In it they recline on couches, find neither the heat of a sun nor bitter cold, receive clustered fruits, and wear silk attire.
Reward is given to the righteous for what they endured, including a Garden, silk attire, and pure drink. Their endeavour upon earth is said to have found acceptance.

l: the way, Surah 76: Man (Al-Insaan), Surah 76: Man (Al-Insaan)
s: The way is shown to man, who may be grateful or disbelieving. This admonishment allows whoever wills to choose a way unto his Lord, though people do not will unless Allah wills.

l: painful doom, Surah 76: Man (Al-Insaan), Surah 76: Man (Al-Insaan)
s: Painful doom is prepared for evil-doers. The unit contrasts this doom with Allah's mercy and the rewards given to the righteous.

l: the day of judgment, Surah 76: Man (Al-Insaan), Surah 76: Man (Al-Insaan)
s: The text refers to a grievous day and a day of frowning and fate that people fear. Allah wards the evil of that day from the righteous, while those who love fleeting life put the remembrance of a grievous day behind them.

l: The Table-Talk of the Prophet Mohammad (Part 1), The Table-Talk of the Prophet Mohammad (Part 1), When God created the creation He wrote a book, which is near him upon the sovran Throne; and what is written in it is this: Verily my compassion overcometh my wrath. .. Of Hospitality
s: This unit concerns God’s compassion, worship, charity, fasting, reading the Korān, honest labour, fighting for the faith, judgment, women and slaves, animals, and hospitality. It describes rewards and punishments connected with prayer, almsgiving, conduct, debt, justice, family relations, and treatment of animals. It also records teachings attributed to the Prophet about social duties, religious observance, and ethical behavior.

l: God, The Table-Talk of the Prophet Mohammad (Part 1), When God created the creation He wrote a book, which is near him upon the sovran Throne; and what is written in it is this: Verily my compassion overcometh my wrath. .. Of Hospitality
s: God is described as compassionate, forgiving, rewarding good deeds, and drawing near to those who approach Him. He loves generosity, purity, liberality, munificence, and good treatment of servants and animals.

l: the Prophet, The Table-Talk of the Prophet Mohammad (Part 1), When God created the creation He wrote a book, which is near him upon the sovran Throne; and what is written in it is this: Verily my compassion overcometh my wrath. .. Of Hospitality
s: The Prophet teaches about worship, charity, fasting, honest work, warfare, judgment, women, slaves, animals, and hospitality. He gives practical instructions, including feeding the hungry, paying labourers, caring for slaves, and protecting noncombatants.

l: the Devil, The Table-Talk of the Prophet Mohammad (Part 1), When God created the creation He wrote a book, which is near him upon the sovran Throne; and what is written in it is this: Verily my compassion overcometh my wrath. .. Of Hospitality
s: The Devil ties three knots upon a sleeping person’s neck and urges continued sleep. He also enters a house where God’s name is not remembered and claims lodging there.

l: Muslims, The Table-Talk of the Prophet Mohammad (Part 1), When God created the creation He wrote a book, which is near him upon the sovran Throne; and what is written in it is this: Verily my compassion overcometh my wrath. .. Of Hospitality
s: Muslims are urged to pray, read the Korān, fast moderately, give charity, work honestly, avoid begging and unlawful gain, repay debts, and treat others and animals well. A Muslim who reads the Korān is compared to an orange fruit with pleasant smell and taste.

l: women, The Table-Talk of the Prophet Mohammad (Part 1), When God created the creation He wrote a book, which is near him upon the sovran Throne; and what is written in it is this: Verily my compassion overcometh my wrath. .. Of Hospitality
s: Women are discussed in relation to marriage, virtue, consent, worship, household conduct, and social leadership. Women are encouraged to give alms, and their homes are described as better for them than mosques.

l: slaves, The Table-Talk of the Prophet Mohammad (Part 1), When God created the creation He wrote a book, which is near him upon the sovran Throne; and what is written in it is this: Verily my compassion overcometh my wrath. .. Of Hospitality
s: Slaves are described as brothers whose owners must provide them with food and clothing and not burden them beyond their power. A person who beats or slaps a slave without fault must free the slave, and ill-treatment of a slave prevents entry into Paradise.

l: judges, The Table-Talk of the Prophet Mohammad (Part 1), When God created the creation He wrote a book, which is near him upon the sovran Throne; and what is written in it is this: Verily my compassion overcometh my wrath. .. Of Hospitality
s: Judges must not decide between two people while angry. Just and unjust judges alike face severe accountability before God, while a just judge is described as experiencing great fear on the Day of Resurrection.

l: Paradise, The Table-Talk of the Prophet Mohammad (Part 1), When God created the creation He wrote a book, which is near him upon the sovran Throne; and what is written in it is this: Verily my compassion overcometh my wrath. .. Of Hospitality
s: Paradise is promised in connection with generosity, virtuous conduct, and certain forms of devotion. The liberal person is described as near Paradise, and a woman whose husband is pleased with her is said to enter it.

l: Hell Fire, The Table-Talk of the Prophet Mohammad (Part 1), When God created the creation He wrote a book, which is near him upon the sovran Throne; and what is written in it is this: Verily my compassion overcometh my wrath. .. Of Hospitality
s: Hell Fire is associated with suicide, stinginess, and mistreatment of slaves. A person who kills himself is described as remaining in Hell Fire everlastingly.

l: the Day of Resurrection, The Table-Talk of the Prophet Mohammad (Part 1), When God created the creation He wrote a book, which is near him upon the sovran Throne; and what is written in it is this: Verily my compassion overcometh my wrath. .. Of Hospitality
s: The Day of Resurrection is presented as a time of judgment, punishment, reward, and divine accountability. Murder is named as the first judgment passed on man, and debts remain serious even for a martyr.

l: prayer, The Table-Talk of the Prophet Mohammad (Part 1), When God created the creation He wrote a book, which is near him upon the sovran Throne; and what is written in it is this: Verily my compassion overcometh my wrath. .. Of Hospitality
s: Prayer is praised as a duty witnessed by angels, and prayers performed in congregation receive double the reward of those said at home. Missed prayers are to be performed when remembered, and prayer is connected with ablution, purity, and charity.

l: charity, The Table-Talk of the Prophet Mohammad (Part 1), When God created the creation He wrote a book, which is near him upon the sovran Throne; and what is written in it is this: Verily my compassion overcometh my wrath. .. Of Hospitality
s: Charity includes almsgiving, justice between people, helping riders and their baggage, kind speech, assisting questioners, walking toward prayer, and removing harmful objects. Giving secretly is highly praised, and generosity is described as bringing God’s pleasure and the friendship of people.

l: fasting, The Table-Talk of the Prophet Mohammad (Part 1), When God created the creation He wrote a book, which is near him upon the sovran Throne; and what is written in it is this: Verily my compassion overcometh my wrath. .. Of Hospitality
s: Fasting is not considered complete when a person continues lying and slandering. The unit recommends moderation, including fasting three days each month while also resting, eating, and fulfilling duties to the body, eyes, wife, visitors, and guests.

l: the Korān, The Table-Talk of the Prophet Mohammad (Part 1), When God created the creation He wrote a book, which is near him upon the sovran Throne; and what is written in it is this: Verily my compassion overcometh my wrath. .. Of Hospitality
s: Reading the Korān is compared to possessing the pleasant qualities of an orange or sweet basil, depending on the reader’s character. It should be read constantly because it is said to run away faster than an untethered camel.

l: labour and profit, The Table-Talk of the Prophet Mohammad (Part 1), When God created the creation He wrote a book, which is near him upon the sovran Throne; and what is written in it is this: Verily my compassion overcometh my wrath. .. Of Hospitality
s: Honest labour and earnings are praised, especially work performed by a person or his children. Begging is discouraged, while truthful trade, avoiding interest and monopoly, relieving debtors, and paying labourers promptly are commanded.

l: fighting for the faith, The Table-Talk of the Prophet Mohammad (Part 1), When God created the creation He wrote a book, which is near him upon the sovran Throne; and what is written in it is this: Verily my compassion overcometh my wrath. .. Of Hospitality
s: Fighting for the faith is described as better than worldly life and prolonged supererogatory prayer. The Prophet instructs armies not to kill old men unable to fight, children, or women, not to steal spoils, and to maintain good relations.

l: judgment, The Table-Talk of the Prophet Mohammad (Part 1), When God created the creation He wrote a book, which is near him upon the sovran Throne; and what is written in it is this: Verily my compassion overcometh my wrath. .. Of Hospitality
s: Judgment includes accountability for murder, suicide, debt, and the conduct of judges. A judge who rules between people is described as being held by the neck before God’s court on the Day of Resurrection.

l: hospitality, The Table-Talk of the Prophet Mohammad (Part 1), When God created the creation He wrote a book, which is near him upon the sovran Throne; and what is written in it is this: Verily my compassion overcometh my wrath. .. Of Hospitality
s: Hospitality requires respecting guests, being kind for one day and one night, entertaining them for three days, and not allowing a guest to remain long enough to inconvenience the host. Remembering God when entering the house and eating prevents the Devil from claiming the house and meal.

l: animals, The Table-Talk of the Prophet Mohammad (Part 1), When God created the creation He wrote a book, which is near him upon the sovran Throne; and what is written in it is this: Verily my compassion overcometh my wrath. .. Of Hospitality
s: Animals must be treated with care, ridden only when fit, and allowed to rest when tired. Good deeds toward animals, including giving them water, are rewarded, and a woman is described as forgiven for giving water to a thirsty dog.

l: debt, The Table-Talk of the Prophet Mohammad (Part 1), When God created the creation He wrote a book, which is near him upon the sovran Throne; and what is written in it is this: Verily my compassion overcometh my wrath. .. Of Hospitality
s: People who owe debts should be given additional time, and forgiving part or all of a debt is praised. Debt is described as so serious that a martyr is forgiven every fault except debt, and refusing to pay when able warrants dishonour and punishment.

Surah 1: The Opening (Al-Faatiha) is revealed at Mecca and concerns worship, praise, and seeking guidance from Allah. Allah is praised as the Lord of the Worlds and as Beneficent and Merciful. The text identifies the Day of Judgment and asks for guidance to the straight path. It distinguishes those who receive favor from those who earn anger or go astray.
Surah 1: The Opening (Al-Faatiha) is revealed at Mecca. It praises Allah, identifies Him as Beneficent and Merciful, declares worship of Him, and asks Him for help and guidance.
Allah is praised as the Lord of the Worlds, the Beneficent, and the Merciful. He alone is worshipped and asked for help, and He is asked to show the straight path.

l: the Day of Judgment, The Opening (Al-Faatiha)
s: The Day of Judgment is identified as a day over which Allah is Master.
The straight path is requested as the way to be shown. It is described as the path of those whom Allah has favoured, rather than those who earn His anger or go astray.

Surah 2: The Cow (Al-Baqara) presents Allah’s guidance, revelation, power, judgment, and commands for mankind. It distinguishes believers, disbelievers, and those who only claim belief; recounts Adam and his wife in the Garden; and follows the Children of Israel through covenant, disobedience, the Exodus, Pharaoh’s drowning, Moses’ command to sacrifice a cow, and Saul’s campaign in which David slew Goliath by Allah’s leave. Abraham’s leadership, the raising of the House with Ishmael, and prayers connected with the Inviolable Place of Worship establish worship and the qiblah. Believers are told to establish worship, pay the poor-due, give charity, fast, seek help through steadfastness and prayer, eat what is lawful, keep treaties, compete in good works, and act patiently and kindly. The text gives guidance on righteousness, pilgrimage, warfare, retaliation, marriage, divorce, nursing, waiting periods, inheritance, charity, usury, and debts. It warns against concealed revelation, inherited error, associating rivals with Allah, sin, aggression, injustice, mischief, covenant-breaking, the Fire, and rejection of faith. It ends with believers affirming faith and seeking forgiveness, mercy, and victory.

Allah is the One Allah, deity, Creator, Originator of the heavens and the earth, and Lord of Abraham. Allah owns the heavens, earth, House, throne, sovereignty, and Hereafter; has no partner; is Alive, Eternal, Merciful, Forgiving, Hearer, Knower, All-Embracing, All-Knowing, Mighty, Wise, and able to do all things. By command, “Be! and it is,” Allah creates mankind, gives life and death, provides manna and quails, and preserves the heavens without weariness. Allah reveals Scripture with truth to Muhammad and mankind, gives revelation, guidance, wisdom, and mercy to whom He wills, and desires ease rather than hardship. Allah knows what souls disclose and hide, sees believers’ deeds, responds to prayer, receives good works, loves beneficence, and is with and blesses steadfast believers. Allah also seals disbelievers’ hearing and hearts, forgives or punishes souls as He wills, and sets duties and limits. The account culminates in the Hereafter, where Allah brings every soul to account and judges Jews, Christians, and people generally on the Day of Resurrection.

Muhammad is a messenger from Allah, sent to mankind with the truth. He receives revelation, recites Allah’s revelations to believers, and teaches them the Scripture and wisdom. He brings glad tidings to believers and warns disbelievers. He is instructed to challenge doubters, turn toward the Inviolable Place of Worship, follow Allah’s guidance, and recognize that Allah, not he, guides people.
Adam, a viceroy on earth, learns all names, dwells in the Garden with his wife, deflects through Satan, receives his Lord’s words, and is forgiven.
Moses, a messenger of Allah, receives Scripture and criterion, leads the Children of Israel through commands and signs, calls for repentance, and conveys the cow sacrifice command.

receive the names [taught by Allah through Adam] The angels question the placing of a viceroy in the earth, then acknowledge that Allah knows what they do not know. They prostrate before Adam, except Iblis, who refuses through pride.

l: Children of Israel, Surah 2: The Cow (Al-Baqara)
s: Children of Israel receive Allah’s covenant and Scripture through Moses, yet worship the calf, seek a king to fight in Allah’s way, and repeatedly turn away, break covenants, and conceal or disbelieve truth.

Mankind is Allah’s creation, called to worship Him and avoid rivals. Originally one community, mankind receives guidance through the messenger, prophets as bearers of good tidings and warners, and Scripture with the truth. It includes believers, disbelievers, and those who claim belief while acting otherwise; some oppose, ask questions, or face affliction. Mankind is made a witness through a middle nation and instructed to follow guidance, eat what is lawful and wholesome, ward off evil, and seek good in this world and the Hereafter.

Believers are a group defined by faith in Allah, the Unseen, the Hereafter, Allah’s revelations, angels, Scripture, prophets, and the Last Day. They are sincere, Allah-fearing, and staunch in love for Allah. Their way unfolds through worship, prayer, steadfastness, remembrance, gratitude, fasting Ramadan when able, giving wealth and the poor-due, spending what Allah provides, keeping treaties, avoiding aggression and usury, recording debts, and observing Allah’s limits. They seek forgiveness and help from Allah, especially through prayer and steadfastness amid affliction. In return, they receive guidance, Allah’s help and protection, blessings, mercy, reward, the firm handhold, and inheritance of the Garden. They are promised Gardens and pure companions, with no fear, grief, or loss.

Disbelievers are in disbelief, do not believe whether warned or not, and are portrayed as deaf, dumb, blind, and lost from the plain road. Their hearing and hearts are sealed, with a covering over their eyes. They are wrong-doers whose patrons are false deities, bringing them from light into darkness. Those who die in disbelief are cursed by Allah, angels, and mankind, and they face a painful, shameful, grievous doom in the Fire, where they abide.
Hypocrites claim belief in Allah and the Last Day, seek to beguile believers, spread mischief while claiming peace, mock believers, and privately declare loyalty to their devils.

Jews are described as denying that Christians follow anything true, refusing to be pleased with Muhammad unless he follows their creed, and being told they cannot properly claim Abraham, Ishmael, Isaac, Jacob, or the tribes.

Christians are said to reject Jewish truth and withhold pleasure from Muhammad unless he follows their creed; they are also told that earlier figures and tribes were not properly claimed as Christians.

afflict Children of Israel [with dreadful torment] Pharaoh's folk afflict the Children of Israel with dreadful torment, slay their sons, and spare their women. Allah delivers the Children of Israel and drowns Pharaoh's folk in the sea.
The Garden, promised to believers who do good works, has flowing rivers, food, pure companions, and everlasting residence.
The Fire is doom prepared for disbelievers, fueled by men and stones; those surrounded by sin or denying Allah's revelations abide therein.

The earth is a resting-place appointed for mankind, containing what they need and belonging to Allah. Mankind is warned against corruption; Allah’s repelling some people by others prevents the earth from being corrupted.

The Hereafter is the certain return of mankind to Allah, where each soul stands without help, accepted intercession, or compensation. It contains the Garden as reward for righteous believers who submit and do good, without fear or grief, and the Fire and unlightened doom as punishment for disbelievers.

The Scripture is revelation revealed with truth, containing guidance and clear proofs for those who ward off evil. It serves as a criterion and judges between mankind concerning their differences. It is read by people of the Scripture, some with the right reading, while others alter, conceal, or cast aside its truth for small gain, leading to disagreement and open schism.

The revelation is truth from Allah, given to Muhammad. It confirms earlier revelation, guides and brings glad tidings to believers, challenges doubters to match a surah, and unfolds through clear recitation, with abrogated or forgotten parts replaced by something better or similar.

Allah’s revelations are clear tokens and portents given for guidance and understanding. They are recited with truth and explained through signs about messengers, belief, worship, charity, usury, debts, and accountability; disbelief, denial despite knowledge, and exchanging them for little are condemned.
The covenant requires worship of Allah alone, kindness, truthful speech, worship, and payment of the poor-due; Allah promises fulfillment but warns the Children of Israel against breaking it.

Guidance comes from Allah through revelation and is itself Allah’s Guidance, distinct from error. Allah makes revelations clear, calls followers to the right way, and guides whom He wills to a straight path. Following it brings success, freedom from fear and grief, and movement from darkness into light; purchasing error instead brings no prosperity, while false deities lead disbelievers into darkness.

Worship is established by believers through devotion to Allah alone: prayer, bowing, prostration, remembrance, thanks, circling the House, and paying the poor-due. It begins with commands to the Children of Israel and unfolds as instructions to believers to avoid rivals with Allah.

is_a sacrifice [commanded by Allah through Moses] The cow is the subject of Allah's command to the people of Moses. It must be neither immature nor with calf, yellow, unyoked, whole, and without mark.

is_a object of worship [chosen by Children of Israel] The Children of Israel choose the calf for worship while Moses is away and thereby wrong themselves. Moses tells them to turn in penitence to their Creator.

is_crossed_by Children of Israel [when Allah rescued them] Allah brings the Children of Israel through the sea and rescues them. Pharaoh's folk are drowned in the sea in the sight of the Children of Israel.

l: the creation of mankind, Surah 2: The Cow (Al-Baqara)
s: is_performed_by Allah Allah creates mankind and those before them and appoints a viceroy in the earth. He teaches Adam the names and declares that He knows what the angels do not know.

l: the Fall of Adam and his wife, Surah 2: The Cow (Al-Baqara)
s: is_caused_by Satan [through deflection from the tree] Adam and his wife are told to dwell in the Garden but not approach a particular tree. Satan causes them to deflect, and they are sent down to the earth, after which Adam receives words and Allah relents toward him.

l: the Exodus from Egypt, Surah 2: The Cow (Al-Baqara)
s: is_a rescue [of Children of Israel from Pharaoh's folk] Allah delivers the Children of Israel from Pharaoh's folk and brings them through the sea. Pharaoh's folk are drowned while the Children of Israel are rescued.

l: the sacrifice of the cow, Surah 2: The Cow (Al-Baqara)
s: is_performed_by Children of Israel [after repeated clarification] Moses tells his people that Allah commands them to sacrifice a cow. After repeatedly asking for details, they sacrifice a cow matching the specified conditions, though they almost do not.

Resurrection is Allah’s giving life after death for the dead. It is demonstrated through a ruined township, people returned after a hundred years, those who fled fearing death, and Abraham’s birds. It unfolds from death to renewed life, signs for understanding, and mankind’s return to Allah.

Sin surrounds wrongdoers who do evil and is linked to mischief, transgression, disobedience, wrongful consumption of property, unjustly changing a will, aggression, disbelief, and selling the Hereafter for worldly life. Though strong drink and games have utility, sin is greater. Accountability rests on what hearts earn, not unintentional oaths.

is_committed_by Children of Israel [after ratifying the covenant] Covenant-breaking includes setting aside a covenant, severing what Allah ordered joined, and failing to uphold commands. The unit attributes loss, ignominy, and punishment to such conduct.

l: people of the Scripture, Surah 2: The Cow (Al-Baqara)
s: People of the Scripture are portrayed as divided: some knowingly conceal truth, oppose believers’ qiblah, and seek their disbelief; others recognize revelation clearly and, reading the Scripture rightly, believe in it.

Abraham fulfills Allah’s commands, is appointed a leader for mankind, and submits to the Lord of the Worlds. With Ishmael, he raises the foundations of the House and prays for its people’s security and provision. He is among the righteous and connected as Ishmael’s father and Isaac’s ancestor.
The House at Makka is a sanctuary, resort, and place of worship for mankind; Abraham and Ishmael are commanded to purify it for those who go around it, meditate, bow, and prostrate.

l: the Inviolable Place of Worship, Surah 2: The Cow (Al-Baqara)
s: The Inviolable Place of Worship is a sanctuary and sacred place in Makka, serving as the qiblah toward which Muhammad and believers turn in prayer. This turning is described as truth from Allah, completing grace and guiding believers. It is also governed by pilgrimage obligations and restrictions on fighting unless opponents attack first.

l: the heavens and the earth, Surah 2: The Cow (Al-Baqara)
s: belong_to Allah The heavens and the earth belong to Allah, who originated them and whose sovereignty encompasses them. Their creation, along with the night and day, water, beasts, winds, clouds, and ships, contains signs for people who have sense.

l: the true religion, Surah 2: The Cow (Al-Baqara)
s: The true religion is Abraham’s upright, non-idolatrous religion, chosen by Allah for his sons and the Children of Israel. Its followers are instructed to remain surrendered to Allah. It has no compulsion: right direction is distinct from error, and rejecting false deities while believing in Allah secures an unbreakable firm handhold.

is_preferred_to disbelief Faith consists of believing in Allah and in what was revealed to Muhammad, Abraham, Ishmael, Isaac, Jacob, the tribes, Moses, Jesus, and the prophets. Those who believe in the like of this faith are rightly guided, while turning away leads to schism.
is_a_choice_against faith Disbelief is chosen instead of faith by those who go astray from a plain road. Those who persist in disbelief until death face Allah’s curse and lasting punishment.

Prayer is worship and a means for believers to seek help with steadfastness and Allah’s companionship. It is performed facing the Inviolable Place of Worship, guarded especially as the midmost prayer, with devotion to Allah; in fear it may be standing or on horseback, followed by remembrance in safety.

is_toward the Inviolable Place of Worship [for prayer] The qiblah is changed to the Inviolable Place of Worship, which becomes the direction for prayer wherever the believers are. The change tests who follows the messenger and is presented as a completion of Allah’s grace and a source of guidance.

l: the Day of Resurrection, Surah 2: The Cow (Al-Baqara)
s: is_a_day_of judgment [concerning disputes] On the Day of Resurrection, Allah judges between Jews and Christians concerning their differences. No soul can avail another, compensation and intercession are not accepted for those who lack Allah’s favor, and those who concealed revelation are not spoken to or made to grow.

Pilgrimage and the visit to Makka are performed for Allah in well-known months, requiring avoidance of lewdness, abuse, and angry conversation while remembering Allah and observing offerings, fasts, and provision for the Hereafter.

l: the signs of Allah, Surah 2: The Cow (Al-Baqara)
s: The signs of Allah encompass creation, changing night and day, ships, rain, revived earth, beasts, winds, clouds, As-Safa, and Al-Marwah.
belongs_to Allah [of the heavens and the earth] The sovereignty belongs to Allah over the heavens and the earth. No guardian or helper exists beside Allah.

are_rewarded_by Allah [when sent before for the soul] Good works include obeying Allah, giving charity, worshiping, submitting to Him, and doing good voluntarily. Whatever good people send ahead for their souls, they will find it with Allah, and those who do good have their reward with their Lord.
The heavens belong to Allah, and His throne includes them. Allah preserves them without weariness.

Wealth is given for love of Allah to kinsfolk, orphans, needy people, wayfarers, those who ask, and for freeing slaves; it is spent in Allah’s cause as an act of good, while wrongful consumption of property is warned against.
The Qur'an, revealed in Ramadan, guides mankind through clear proofs and a criterion distinguishing right from wrong, unfolding with righteousness beyond turning faces East or West.

Women have rights similar to men’s in kindness. They observe specified waiting periods after divorce or a husband’s death, abstain from intercourse during menstruation until purified, are described as tilth for husbands, and must be treated honorably in divorce.
Ramadan is a month in which the Qur'an was revealed; those present fast, while the sick and travelers fast an equal number of other days.

Fasting is prescribed for believers, as for those before them, to ward off evil. Sick people and travelers may make up days; certain people may provide a ransom. At night, intercourse, eating, and drinking are permitted until dawn.
Retaliation in murder is prescribed, allows forgiveness, prosecution according to usage, and kind payment; it is described as preserving life for people of understanding.

Fighting is ordained for believers but restricted by nonaggression: they must not initiate hostilities or fight in an inviolable place unless attacked. It is permitted against those who fight, while warfare in the sacred month is a grave transgression. Fighting in Allah’s way is commanded, illustrated by Saul’s steadfast small company defeating a mighty host.

Almsgiving is a good deed for Allah’s pleasure, encouraged through giving good things to help the poor. Allah multiplies its reward, while injury, reproach, ostentation, and inferior gifts diminish or invalidate it.

Marriage with idolaters and idolatresses is prohibited until they believe; believing bondwomen and slaves are preferred, while marital relations, nursing, engagement, and reconciliation are also addressed.
Divorce is pronounced twice and regulated by waiting periods, fair provision, and kind retention or release; harming divorced women or obstructing remarriage is forbidden.

l: the Last Day, Surah 2: The Cow (Al-Baqara)
s: The Last Day has no trafficking, friendship, or intercession except by Allah's leave, and every soul receives what it has earned.
Saul is raised by Allah as king over the Children of Israel, gains a kingdom, tests his army at a river, and leads them against Goliath and his hosts.
The poor are intended charity recipients: constrained in Allah’s cause, unable to travel for trade, and not begging persistently; charity given to them is better when concealed.

l: the Day of Judgment, Surah 2: The Cow (Al-Baqara)
s: The Day of Judgment is described as the day when people are brought back to Allah and every soul is paid in full for what it earned, without being wronged.
Usury is forbidden and unfruitful; trade is permitted. Allah blights it, commands believers to abandon it, and warns unrepentant people of war from Allah and His messenger.
A debt for a fixed term is recorded in writing by a just scribe and witnessed; if the debtor is in hardship, repayment is postponed until ease, while remitting it as charity is better.

Surah 3, The Family of Imraan, presents Allah’s sovereignty, creation, mercy, guidance, warnings, and final judgment through the contrast between belief and disbelief. It addresses Muhammad, the Scripture, earlier revelations, believers, disbelievers, the People of the Scripture, messengers, and hypocrites. It recounts the family of 'Imran, Mary, Zachariah, John, Jesus son of Mary, and the disciples, and affirms Abraham, the Torah, Gospel, Becca, and pilgrimage. It then commands believers to hold fast to Allah, obey the messenger, endure trials, seek forgiveness, and recalls Badr and Uhud, ending with paradise, the Fire, death, resurrection, and accountability.

l: Allah, Surah 3: The Family of Imraan (Aal-i-Imraan)
s: Allah is the only God: Alive, Eternal, Almighty, Wise, Creator, and owner of the heavens and earth, knowing all that is hidden and apparent. Allah gives life and death, sustenance, sovereignty, honor, and abasement as He wills; guides, forgives, judges, tests, helps, rewards, and severely punishes according to what people do. He loves the good, those who trust Him, and believers who follow Muhammad, but does not love disbelievers in His guidance. Allah preferred Adam, Noah, the Family of Abraham, and the Family of 'Imran; accepted, chose, purified, and preferred Mary; gave her tidings of the Messiah; taught and raised Jesus, cleansed him of disbelievers, and set believers above them until the Day of Resurrection. He gathers mankind to an undoubted Day and is the best of helpers and schemers.

l: Muhammad, Surah 3: The Family of Imraan (Aal-i-Imraan)
s: Muhammad is Allah’s messenger who receives, recites, and teaches the Scripture and wisdom to believers. He is instructed to call people to Allah, convey and follow Allah’s guidance, invite the People of the Scripture to agreement, consult believers, pardon them, seek forgiveness for them, and trust in Allah despite those who turn away or hasten to disbelief.

l: Allah's revelations, Surah 3: The Family of Imraan (Aal-i-Imraan)
s: Allah's revelations are a Scripture revealed with truth to Muhammad, confirming the Torah and Gospel. They contain clear guidance and allegorical passages. Believers recite them truthfully and follow them as righteous; people must not conceal, distort, or exploit them for dissension, lest disbelievers face punishment.

l: the Torah, Surah 3: The Family of Imraan (Aal-i-Imraan)
s: The Torah was revealed by Allah before the Gospel. Jesus confirms what was before him of the Torah, and the text challenges the People of the Scripture to produce and read it.

l: the Gospel, Surah 3: The Family of Imraan (Aal-i-Imraan)
s: The Gospel was revealed by Allah after the Torah. Jesus confirms what was before him of the Torah and is taught the Torah and the Gospel.

l: the revelations of Allah, Surah 3: The Family of Imraan (Aal-i-Imraan)
s: are_disbelieved_in_by the disbelievers The revelations of Allah are disbelieved, distorted, or knowingly concealed by some people. Those who disbelieve them are warned of severe punishment.

l: mankind, Surah 3: The Family of Imraan (Aal-i-Imraan)
s: is_attracted_to the joys of women and offspring [as well as wealth, horses, cattle and land] Mankind is created by Allah, and Allah knows what is in the heavens, the earth, and people’s breasts. Mankind is attracted to women, offspring, wealth, horses, cattle, and land, but a better abode is promised with Allah.

l: the believers, Surah 3: The Family of Imraan (Aal-i-Imraan)
s: The believers are those who surrender to and believe in Allah, follow Muhammad as the messenger, and are guided by Allah’s revelations. They obey Allah, pray, seek forgiveness, remain steadfast, hold fast together to Allah’s cable, enjoin right conduct and forbid indecency. They spend without hoarding in ease and adversity, control wrath, forgive mankind, and trust Allah. Allah protects and helps them, granting forgiveness, mercy, victory, guidance, and vast full reward.

l: the disbelievers, Surah 3: The Family of Imraan (Aal-i-Imraan)
s: The disbelievers reject Allah’s revelations and oppose Him. Their wealth, progeny, schemes, and brief worldly comfort will not avail them or harm Allah. They face terror and punishment, are overcome and gathered toward Hell, where the Fire is their habitation, and are deprived of a portion in the Hereafter.

l: People of the Scripture, Surah 3: The Family of Imraan (Aal-i-Imraan)
s: People of the Scripture receive the Scripture but differ after knowledge through transgression. They are warned against hiding, distorting, and concealing Allah’s revelations and against turning believers away. Though some oppose believers, others are trustworthy and steadfast: they recite revelations at night, believe in Allah and the Last Day, promote right conduct, forbid indecency, compete in good works, humble themselves before Allah, and receive His reward.

l: the angels, Surah 3: The Family of Imraan (Aal-i-Imraan)
s: The angels witness that there is no god save Allah, support believers in battle, give Zachariah glad tidings of John, and tell Mary that Allah chose and purified her.

l: the Children of Israel, Surah 3: The Family of Imraan (Aal-i-Imraan)
s: receive the Torah [before the Gospel] Jesus is sent as a messenger to the Children of Israel with signs from Allah. He confirms the Torah, makes lawful some things previously forbidden, and calls them to keep their duty to Allah and obey him.

l: the prophets, Surah 3: The Family of Imraan (Aal-i-Imraan)
s: Some people are condemned for wrongfully slaying the prophets. Allah makes a covenant with the prophets that they will believe in and support a later messenger who confirms what they possess.

l: the disciples, Surah 3: The Family of Imraan (Aal-i-Imraan)
s: are Allah's helpers [they believe in Allah and have surrendered] The disciples answer Jesus’s call for helpers in the cause of Allah. They say that they believe in Allah, follow the messenger sent by Allah, and ask to be enrolled among witnesses to the truth.

l: the Family of 'Imran, Surah 3: The Family of Imraan (Aal-i-Imraan)
s: Allah prefers the Family of 'Imran above the creatures, along with Adam, Noah, and the Family of Abraham. Mary is connected to this family through the account of 'Imran’s wife and her consecrated child.

l: Abraham, Surah 3: The Family of Imraan (Aal-i-Imraan)
s: is_a upright man [having surrendered to Allah and not being an idolater] Abraham is described as an upright man who surrendered to Allah and was not an idolater. The text says that those with the best claim to him are those who followed him, Muhammad, and the believers.

l: Mary, Surah 3: The Family of Imraan (Aal-i-Imraan)
s: Mary, mother of Jesus, is protected from Satan, accepted and given goodly growth; Allah chooses and purifies her, then gives her tidings of the Messiah, Jesus.

l: Zachariah, Surah 3: The Family of Imraan (Aal-i-Imraan)
s: is guardian of Mary Zachariah becomes Mary’s guardian and finds food with her that Allah provides. He prays for offspring, receives glad tidings of John, and is given a sign that he will not speak to mankind for three days except by signs.

l: John, Surah 3: The Family of Imraan (Aal-i-Imraan)
s: is_a prophet [of the righteous] John is announced to Zachariah as a son whose name is John. He will confirm a word from Allah, be lordly and chaste, and be a prophet of the righteous.

l: Hell, Surah 3: The Family of Imraan (Aal-i-Imraan)
s: is_a resting-place [evil] Hell is the destination described for those who disbelieve, and it is called an evil resting-place. The disbelievers are gathered to it and become fuel for the Fire.

l: the Fire, Surah 3: The Family of Imraan (Aal-i-Imraan)
s: The Fire is a punishment and heavy doom prepared for disbelievers, their habitation and fuelled by their wealth and progeny. Believers ask Allah to guard them from it. Some falsely claim it will touch them only for certain days; removal from it and entry into paradise is triumph.

l: the Hereafter, Surah 3: The Family of Imraan (Aal-i-Imraan)
s: contains the Gardens [for those who keep from evil] The Hereafter contains judgment, reward, punishment, and loss for those who reject surrender to Allah. Believers receive their wages in full, while disbelievers and wrongdoers are warned of painful doom.

l: the Gardens, Surah 3: The Family of Imraan (Aal-i-Imraan)
s: The Gardens are a place promised and prepared for those who keep from or ward off evil. Rivers flow beneath them, and they are as wide as the heavens and earth. Their recipients abide there forever with pure companions and Allah’s contentment, as a welcome and reward from Allah.

l: Becca, Surah 3: The Family of Imraan (Aal-i-Imraan)
s: is the first Sanctuary appointed for mankind [a blessed place and a guidance to the peoples] Becca is described as the site of the first Sanctuary appointed for mankind. It is blessed and a guidance to the peoples.

l: the House, Surah 3: The Family of Imraan (Aal-i-Imraan)
s: is a place of pilgrimage [pilgrimage to it is a duty for those able to find a way] The House contains plain memorials of Allah’s guidance and the place where Abraham stood to pray. Pilgrimage to it is a duty owed to Allah for those who are able to find a way there, and whoever enters it is safe.

l: the Day of Resurrection, Surah 3: The Family of Imraan (Aal-i-Imraan)
s: The Day of Resurrection is a day of judgment when Allah gathers people, judges their differences, and all return to Him. Every soul is fully repaid for its earnings; embezzlers bring what they embezzled. Belief and deeds determine outcomes, including whitened or blackened faces.

l: the Day of Judgment, Surah 3: The Family of Imraan (Aal-i-Imraan)
s: The Day of Judgment is not named in the text. The unit does describe a day on which every soul is paid in full for what it has earned and is confronted with its good and evil deeds.

l: religion, Surah 3: The Family of Imraan (Aal-i-Imraan)
s: is the Surrender to Allah's Will and Guidance [with Allah] Religion with Allah is surrender to His will and guidance. The text rejects seeking a religion other than surrender to Allah and calls people to worship Him alone.

l: guidance, Surah 3: The Family of Imraan (Aal-i-Imraan)
s: belongs_to Allah Guidance comes from Allah, the Scripture, and the clear revelations. Those who surrender are rightly guided, while Allah does not guide wrongdoing people or those who disbelieve after clear proofs.

l: belief and disbelief, Surah 3: The Family of Imraan (Aal-i-Imraan)
s: Belief is faith in Allah and His revelations, shown through following the messenger, obedience, steadfastness, prayer, spending, and forgiveness. Believers seek strengthened hearts and truth, are tested and distinguished by Allah, and receive reward; disbelief and wrongdoing lead to repentance or to loss, terror, punishment, and the Fire.

l: disbelief, Surah 3: The Family of Imraan (Aal-i-Imraan)
s: leads_to a painful doom [when maintained until death] Disbelief includes rejecting Allah’s revelations, turning away after clear proofs, and denying the truth knowingly. It brings loss in the world and the Hereafter, punishment, and exclusion from Allah’s guidance.

l: the revelation of Jesus, Surah 3: The Family of Imraan (Aal-i-Imraan)
s: The revelation of Jesus is not separately named in the text. Jesus is described as receiving the Scripture, wisdom, the Torah, and the Gospel, and as bringing signs from Allah.

l: the birth of Jesus, Surah 3: The Family of Imraan (Aal-i-Imraan)
s: The birth of Jesus is announced to Mary as the creation of a child without a mortal touching her. Allah creates what He wills and says to a thing, 'Be,' and it is.

l: the crucifixion and ascension of Jesus, Surah 3: The Family of Imraan (Aal-i-Imraan)
s: The text does not mention the crucifixion of Jesus. It states that Allah gathered Jesus, caused him to ascend to Allah, cleansed him of those who disbelieved, and set his followers above the disbelievers until the Day of Resurrection.

l: messengers, Surah 3: The Family of Imraan (Aal-i-Imraan)
s: Messengers are sent by Allah but denied by disbelievers; before Muhammad, some brought miracles, Psalms, and Scripture and were slain, while believers are promised reward for faith and duty.

l: the hypocrites, Surah 3: The Family of Imraan (Aal-i-Imraan)
s: The hypocrites are nearer to disbelief than faith, hiding thoughts within themselves; they claim willingness to fight or defend themselves, but withdraw when fighting occurs, speaking contrary to their hearts.

l: the best community, Surah 3: The Family of Imraan (Aal-i-Imraan)
s: The best community is raised up for mankind, believing in Allah and distinguished by enjoining right conduct and forbidding indecency; it is presented as superior in purpose and conduct while many People of the Scripture are evil-livers.

l: the cable of Allah, Surah 3: The Family of Imraan (Aal-i-Imraan)
s: is_held_fast_to believers [together] The cable of Allah is to be held fast by all believers together, and they are told not to separate. Allah's favor made former enemies into brothers and saved them from the brink of an abyss of fire.

l: the heavens and the earth, Surah 3: The Family of Imraan (Aal-i-Imraan)
s: belong_to Allah The heavens and the earth belong to Allah, and their creation, along with the difference of night and day, contains signs for people of understanding. They are described as vast in relation to paradise, and Allah is their Sovereign.

l: the battle, Surah 3: The Family of Imraan (Aal-i-Imraan)
s: tests believers The battle includes Allah's support for believers at Badr with angels and the testing of believers at Uhud. At Uhud, some believers disobeyed, disputed, fled, grieved, and were later forgiven, while the events distinguished true believers from hypocrites.

l: death, Surah 3: The Family of Imraan (Aal-i-Imraan)
s: Death is tasted by every soul only by Allah’s leave at an appointed term; whether death or being slain in Allah’s way, it is followed by pardon, mercy, gathering to Him, or provision.

l: right conduct and indecency, Surah 3: The Family of Imraan (Aal-i-Imraan)
s: are_contrasted one another [right conduct is enjoined and indecency is forbidden] Right conduct is to be enjoined, and indecency is to be forbidden. Those who practice right conduct, avoid indecency, and compete in good works are counted among the successful and righteous.

l: forgiveness, Surah 3: The Family of Imraan (Aal-i-Imraan)
s: Forgiveness is sought from Allah for sins and granted to those who repent, remember Allah, seek forgiveness, and do not knowingly repeat wrongs; Allah also forgave believers who turned back at Uhud.

l: Allah's help, Surah 3: The Family of Imraan (Aal-i-Imraan)
s: enables believers [to overcome opponents] Allah's help gave believers victory at Badr and support through angels, and it is presented as the source of victory. If Allah helps believers, none can overcome them; if He withdraws His help, no one can help them after Him.

l: the believers at Uhud, Surah 3: The Family of Imraan (Aal-i-Imraan)
s: The believers at Uhud are tested through loss of courage, dispute, disobedience, worldly desire, and flight while Muhammad calls them. After grief, Allah sends security, exposes hypocrites, forgives those who turn back, and teaches that the disaster connects to their actions.

This document summarizes Surah 4, The Women (An-Nisaa), revealed at Medina. It addresses mankind and believers with commands from Allah concerning faith, justice, family life, wealth, worship, conflict, and the Last Day. It begins with duty to Allah, protection of orphans and their property, and detailed inheritance shares for children, parents, spouses, siblings, and distant kindred. It regulates marriage, dowries, prohibited relations, treatment of wives, female orphans, divorce or reconciliation, and arbitration between spouses. It condemns wrongful wealth-taking, killing, lewdness, treachery, false accusation, pride, hoarding, and injustice, while emphasizing repentance and Allah’s forgiveness under stated conditions. Believers are commanded to serve Allah alone, show kindness to relatives, neighbors, travellers, and dependents, return deposits, judge fairly, and stand firmly for justice even against themselves or kin. The text gives directions for prayer, purification, travel, and worship amid danger. It addresses obedience to Allah, the messenger, and authority, the handling of disputes, migration, military precautions, fighting for oppressed people, and penalties for mistaken or intentional killing. Hypocrites and disbelievers are portrayed as deceptive, wavering, obstructive, or hostile; believers are warned against choosing disbelievers over believers. The People of the Scripture are reproached for demands, covenant-breaking, distortion, and disbelief, while Moses, Jesus son of Mary, Abraham, Muhammad, and other messengers are mentioned. The surah repeatedly contrasts Fire, painful doom, and hell for disbelief, transgression, hypocrisy, and ascribing partners to Allah with eternal Gardens, reward, mercy, pure companions, and shade for those who believe, obey, repent, and do good works. It closes by affirming Allah’s oneness, knowledge, authority over heaven and earth, the messenger’s truth, and final inheritance guidance.

l: Surah 4: The Women (An-Nisaa), Surah 4: The Women (An-Nisaa)
s: A surah revealed at Medina, addressing mankind’s duty to Allah through creation, care for orphans and women, marriage, inheritance, and justice, and warning that wrongful consumption of orphans’ wealth brings burning flame.

Allah is the sole deity, creator of mankind from a single soul and its mate, owner of the heavens and earth, and watcher, witness, guardian, supporter, defender, reckoner, and judge. Allah is repeatedly described as knowing, wise, aware, hearing, seeing, merciful, forgiving, mighty, powerful, high, exalted, great, truthful, all-embracing, and sufficient. Allah knows and surrounds all deeds, secret plans, sin, faith, and all things; does not wrong even an ant’s weight; doubles good deeds; and gives immense reward. The record unfolds through Allah’s ordering of human life: provision and inheritance for children, parents, spouses, and distant kindred; rules concerning women, marriage, dowries, lewdness, orphans, deposits, worship, justice, and judgment. Allah explains guidance, lightens burdens, appoints ways, commands fairness, and makes disputing spouses of one mind if they seek amendment. Believers are called to serve Allah without partners, uphold justice, believe in Allah and the messengers, and do good. Allah grants Scripture and wisdom, reveals Scripture to Muhammad, gives decree concerning women, and bestowed Scripture, wisdom, and a mighty kingdom upon the house of Abraham. Allah chose Abraham as a friend, bestowed authority on Moses, and took Jesus son of Mary unto Himself. Allah rewards obedience, belief, good works, migration, and seeking His good pleasure with forgiveness, mercy, Gardens, and reward in the world and Hereafter. Allah may pardon those who repent or are oppressed, but does not pardon partners ascribed unto Him except as He wills. Allah curses and punishes disbelief, wrongdoing, treachery, intentional killing, and rejection of guidance. In the end, Allah gathers mankind for the Day of Resurrection and judges hypocrites, disbelievers, and all people justly.

Mankind is a multitude that includes men and women. It is created by Allah from a single soul and receives Allah's bounty, though some are jealous of what Allah has bestowed upon it and would withhold even the speck on a date-stone if they shared in the Sovereignty. Mankind is told to be careful of its duty toward Allah, the wombs, and claims of rights over one another, and to speak kindly and justly. Muhammad is instructed to judge between mankind by the truth Allah shows in the Scripture. Messengers are sent so that mankind will have no argument against Allah after them. At the close, mankind is told that the messenger has come with Truth from its Lord and is urged to believe, because belief is better for it; even if it disbelieves, whatever is in the heavens and earth belongs to Allah, the Knower and Wise.

Men are described as having earned fortunes, being in charge of women, and providing women financial support. Their authority is attributed to Allah making some excel others and to their spending of property for women’s support. Men may also be feeble and unable to devise a plan or find a way. The records culminate by restating their described authority and financial role.

Women are presented through legal, moral, and marital provisions. They receive marriage portions as free gifts and may freely remit part of them. They are assigned a legal inheritance share from parents and near kindred; when more than two, they collectively receive two-thirds. They may possess a fortune from their own earnings. Good women are described as obedient and as guarding in secret what Allah has guarded. The records also set out a punishment for women found guilty of lewdness: four witnesses must testify to the allegation, after which the women are confined to houses until death or until Allah appoints another way. Across the records, women appear first as recipients and holders of property, then as subjects of legal accusation and confinement, and finally within expectations of obedience and private guardianship.

Orphans possess wealth and heritage that must be safeguarded. They are to receive their wealth when they reach marriageable age, show sound judgment, and are present at its division. People must protect them through just behavior, give them just treatment, and avoid exchanging, absorbing, squandering, or wrongfully consuming their wealth. The records begin with their wealth and inheritance, set conditions for receiving it, warn against wrongful consumption, and conclude with a command to deal justly with orphans, noting that Allah is aware of good done for them.

Wealth is property that may belong to orphans, be exchanged in trade by mutual consent, be hoarded, or be spent. Orphans’ wealth must be maintained, kept separate from guardians’ wealth, and delivered when appropriate; those kept from managing it are still to be fed, clothed, and addressed kindly. Among believers, wealth must not be squandered in vanity, though mutually consenting trade is permitted. Some disbelievers hoard wealth, encourage avarice, conceal what Allah bestowed, or spend it to be seen by people. The records contrast these practices with spending Allah’s wealth aright.

Parents are heirs in inheritance provisions. When their child dies leaving a son, each parent receives one-sixth after any legacy or debt. If there is no son and the parents are heirs, the mother receives one-third; if there are brethren, her share is one-sixth. The provision is presented as an injunction from Allah, who is Knower and Wise, alongside a warning that disobeying Allah and His messenger and transgressing limits leads to Fire and shameful doom.

Heritage is a legal share left by parents and near kindred and allotted to men and women, whether little or much. Kinsfolk, orphans, and the needy who are present when it is divided are to receive something. Its central matter is the prescribed distribution among children, parents, spouses, and certain distant heirs, with legacies and debts settled first. For children, a male receives the equivalent of two females; one woman receives half, while more than two women receive two-thirds. Parents may receive sixths, while the mother may receive a third or a sixth according to the stated heirs. The pronouncement concerning distant kindred concludes with the childless-man case: a sister receives half, two sisters receive two-thirds, and where there are brethren, men and women, the male receives the equivalent of two females.
Mankind is told to be careful of its duty toward Allah, toward the wombs, and in its treatment of orphans. Those responsible for orphans are told to mind their duty to Allah and speak justly.

Justice is required in dealing with orphans and in marriage. If a person fears being unable to deal justly with multiple women, the text directs him to marry one only or those whom his right hand possesses. Justice requires believers to give truthful witness for Allah even when the matter concerns themselves, their parents, their kindred, a rich man, or a poor man. Believers are warned not to follow passion and thereby lapse from truth.

requires justice [when marrying multiple women] Marriage is discussed in relation to women, marriageable age, fairness, and marriage portions. Marriage to two, three, or four women is permitted if fairness can be maintained, but one is directed if justice cannot be done.

Sin is committed only against oneself. The records warn believers against injustice and constraint in marriage, urge kindness, and present marriage to believing maids for one who fears sin, while saying patience is better. They condemn deceit, treachery, and ascribing partners unto Allah, which is not pardoned. Yet one who commits a sin and seeks Allah's pardon can find Allah Forgiving and Merciful.
Fire is what those who wrongfully devour orphans’ wealth swallow into their bellies; it then leads to their exposure to burning flame.

Muhammad is Allah’s messenger unto mankind, made a witness against people who disbelieved and disobeyed the messenger. He is to be obeyed together with Allah, and believers in Allah and the Last Day accept his decisions with full submission. He judges disputes and mankind by what Allah shows him through the Scripture revealed with truth. Allah also gives him wisdom, grace, mercy, and teaching of what he did not know. The records present Muhammad’s role in guidance, judgment, worship, and struggle. He arranges worship for believers when among them, is told to judge justly, not to plead for the treacherous, and to seek Allah’s forgiveness. He is told to fight in Allah’s way, urge believers onward, oppose people secretly planning against his instructions, and trust Allah. Although he is charged with these tasks, he bears responsibility only for himself. His authority is linked to Allah’s commands and limits: obeying Allah and His messenger brings believers among those shown favour, while disobeying the messenger and transgressing Allah’s limits leads to Fire and a shameful doom. Muhammad’s position unfolds as that of a recipient of revelation, wisdom, grace, and mercy; a judge guided by the revealed Scripture; a leader directing believers in worship and action; and a messenger whose obedience and judgments are integral to belief and accountability before Allah.

Children are addressed in Allah’s inheritance provisions. A male child receives the equivalent of two female portions. If there is one female child, her share is half; if there are more than two female children, their share is two-thirds. The provisions also set shares for parents, depending on whether the deceased has children or brethren, after legacies and debts. The passage says people do not know which parents or children are nearer in usefulness, calls the rule an injunction from Allah, and warns that disobeying Allah and His messenger brings Fire and a shameful doom.

The male is an heir among brethren, men and women. When inheritance is divided, he receives a share equivalent to that of two females. This rule appears within a pronouncement concerning distant kindred and childless deaths, where sisters’ shares are also specified, and concludes with Allah’s explanation so that people do not err.

A group of two females is defined through inheritance shares. Each female receives half the portion of a male, so together their shares equal one male's share. The record situates this rule within a pronouncement on distant kindred: when brethren include men and women, the male receives the equivalent of the share of two females. It begins with the share relation and concludes by confirming the two females' combined equivalence to one male.
The presence of a son affects the inheritance shares of parents and spouses. A son causes each parent to receive a sixth and reduces the spouse's share as specified.

receives_share inheritance [one-third when there is no son and the parents are heirs] The mother receives a third when there is no son and the parents are the heirs. She receives a sixth when the deceased has brethren.

l: injunction from Allah, Surah 4: The Women (An-Nisaa)
s: is_a injunction The inheritance provisions for parents and children are identified as an injunction from Allah. The text states that Allah knows which of them is nearer in usefulness.

Man is described as created weak; therefore Allah would make the burden light for him. In inheritance, as a husband, he receives one-half if his wife has no child. He is also addressed in rules forbidding forcible inheritance of women and requiring kind consort.

Women are presented chiefly in relation to marriage, inheritance, and household conflict. A wife may receive an inheritance share, money or gifts from her husband, and a strong pledge through marriage, yet she is also described as potentially weak or unable to plan. The account rejects forcibly inheriting women and constraining them to recover what husbands gave them; husbands are instructed to live with wives kindly, and gifts should not be reclaimed merely because a husband seeks another wife. It then addresses feared rebellion by wives through admonition, separation in beds, and scourging, while barring further action if they obey; disputes between spouses may involve arbiters from each family. Finally, women are subjects of consultation and divine decree, including female orphans and weak children. A wife fearing mistreatment or desertion may negotiate peaceful terms with her husband.

l: commandment from Allah, Surah 4: The Women (An-Nisaa)
s: is_a commandment The rules for shares of distant heirs are identified as a commandment from Allah. The commandment is given with provisions concerning legacies and debts.

l: limits imposed by Allah, Surah 4: The Women (An-Nisaa)
s: are_set_by Allah The inheritance rules are described as limits imposed by Allah. Whoever obeys Allah and His messenger enters Gardens, while whoever transgresses these limits enters Fire.

Fire is an eternal dwelling and destination for those who disobey Allah and His messenger, transgress Allah's limits, or disbelieve Allah's revelations. It brings a shameful doom and torments disbelievers by renewing their skins after they are consumed. Its lowest deep contains hypocrites, who have no helper except those who repent and amend. From the beginning, Fire is identified as the lasting destination of disobedience; it then unfolds as punishment through torment and renewed skins, ending with hypocrites confined to its lowest deep without help unless they repent and amend.

Gardens are an eternal dwelling promised by Allah. Rivers flow underneath them, and they are for those who obey Allah and His messenger, believe, and do good works. Their inhabitants will dwell there forever, with pure companions and plenteous shade. Entering these Gardens is called the great success, while disobeying Allah and His messenger and transgressing His limits leads instead to Fire and a shameful doom.
A shameful doom is prepared by Allah for disbelievers: those who disbelieve in Allah and His messengers and seek a way between belief and disbelief.

l: people guilty of lewdness, Surah 4: The Women (An-Nisaa)
s: People guilty of lewdness are subject to testimony and punishment. Women may be confined after four witnesses testify, until death or new legislation provides another way. The guilty may be released or left alone if they repent and improve, while repentance at death is not accepted and disbelievers who die face painful doom.

Lewdness is treated as an offense requiring four witnesses against women accused of it and punishment for the two guilty of it. Flagrant lewdness is an exception to the prohibition against constraining the women of deceased kinsmen. Lewdness is also identified with forbidden sexual conduct and results in punishment for a believing maid who commits it after marriage.

Death is presented as ending the confinement of women found guilty of lewdness, unless Allah appoints another way. It also attends people who have done ill-deeds: repentance declared only then is excluded from forgiveness. Those who die while disbelievers likewise receive a painful doom.
A believing maid who commits lewdness after honorable marriage incurs half of the punishment prescribed for free women.

Repentance is accepted for those who do evil in ignorance and then turn quickly to Allah. It is incumbent on Allah for them. The account contrasts this with those who continue ill-deeds until death attends them and then repent, and with those who die as disbelievers; neither receives the stated forgiveness, and painful doom is prepared for the latter.

Forgiveness concerns Allah’s pardon for wrongdoing and the conditions under which it is granted or withheld. It is incumbent toward people who do evil in ignorance, repent quickly, and improve, and it may be sought by those who do evil or wrong their own souls. Allah is forgiving and merciful, may pardon feeble men, women, and children unable to devise a plan or find a way, and promises pardon alongside the reward of those who strive. Yet forgiveness is not for evil deeds when repentance is delayed until death attends, nor for those who die while disbelieving. Allah pardons all save ascribing partners unto Him, except whom He wills. The account thus moves from repentance and improvement, through Allah’s mercy and pardon, to firm limits on delayed repentance, disbelief, and ascribing partners.

is_done_in ignorance [by those toward whom Allah relents] Those who do evil in ignorance may receive forgiveness if they quickly turn in repentance to Allah. Evil deeds followed by repentance at the time of death do not receive the stated forgiveness.

Disbelievers are characterized by rejection of Allah, the Last Day, Allah’s messengers, and revelations; some seek a position between belief and disbelief or distinguish among messengers. They may hoard wealth, urge avarice, conceal Allah’s bounty, and spend to be seen by men. They fight for idols, hinder Allah’s way, reject and deride revelations, and are an open enemy to believers, hoping believers neglect arms and baggage so they can attack. Believers are warned not to choose them as friends in place of believers or sit with them while they deride revelations. Disbelievers seek friendship with power and will be gathered with hypocrites into hell. Their course is described as far astray: those who disbelieve and deal in wrong are neither forgiven nor guided except to hell, where they abide forever. They are prepared for and receive shameful doom; after disobeying the messenger, they will wish to be level with the ground and will be unable to hide any fact from Allah.

Believers are a group addressed through commands, prohibitions, promises, and warnings. They are directed to act fairly in marriage and wealth: not to forcibly inherit or constrain women, to consort with them kindly, fulfill marriage portions, avoid vain squandering, and not kill one another. Their worship requires care: they must not approach prayer while drunken or polluted, and may use high clean soil when water is unavailable in specified circumstances. Those who believe and do good works are promised eternal Gardens, pure companions, and plenteous shade. They must obey Allah and the messenger, refer disputes to them, and submit to the messenger’s judgment. Obedience places them with those shown Allah’s favour. They are called to take precautions, advance in groups or together, fight for Allah’s cause, avoid intentional killing of another believer, and carefully distinguish those offering peace rather than calling them disbelievers. Those striving with wealth and lives receive higher rank and reward. Believers must be staunch witnesses for Allah in justice, even against themselves, parents, or kindred, and must not follow passion away from truth. They are commanded to believe in Allah, Muhammad, angels, scriptures, messengers, and the Last Day; to accept Allah’s messengers without distinction; and to believe in revelations sent to Muhammad and before him. They are warned against choosing disbelievers as friends in place of believers and are promised immense reward, particularly alongside prayer, poor-due, and belief in Allah and the Last Day.

l: women (of your deceased kinsmen), Surah 4: The Women (An-Nisaa)
s: The women of deceased kinsmen must not be forcibly inherited or constrained so that part of what was given to them can be taken away, unless they are guilty of flagrant lewdness.
is_forbidden_to believers [except captives whom their right hands possess] Married women are forbidden in marriage, except those captives whom the right hands possess.
Honest wedlock is the lawful form of seeking women with wealth, as opposed to debauchery. Those married in this way are to receive their portions as a duty.

Believing maids are women who may be married by believers unable to afford free believing women. Their folk must grant permission, and they must receive portions in kindness after honorable marriage. They are expected to be honest rather than debauched or of loose conduct. If they commit lewdness after honorable marriage, they incur half the punishment prescribed for free women. The record places these rules alongside commands against forcibly inheriting or constraining women and for consorting with them in kindness.
cause believers [to go tremendously astray] Those who follow vain desires want believers to go tremendously astray.
is_upon Muhammad Allah turns to believers in mercy and is described as Merciful.
Allah's guidance is manifested to the messenger's opponents before they oppose him. Opposing the messenger after that manifestation leads to following another way and exposure to hell.
requires mutual consent Trade by mutual consent is permitted among believers.

Men who are husbands are instructed to admonish women from whom they fear rebellion, banish them to beds apart, and scourge them. If the women obey, the men must not seek a way against them. Husbands are addressed concerning ill treatment, desertion, and unequal treatment of wives. They cannot deal equally between their wives, however much they wish, and they are told not to turn altogether away from one wife.

is_faced_by men (husbands) [when feared in women (wives)] When rebellion is feared from women, admonition, separation in beds, and scourging are prescribed. If the women obey, no further way may be sought against them.

Marital breach is a feared conflict between husband and wife. It is addressed by appointing one arbiter from his folk and one from her folk; if they seek amendment, Allah will make the couple of one mind.
is_appointed_from his folk [to address marital breach] An arbiter from the man's folk is appointed when a breach is feared between the man and wife.
is_appointed_from her folk [to address marital breach] An arbiter from the woman's folk is appointed when a breach is feared between the man and wife.
is_desired_by arbiter (his folk) [together with the arbiter from her folk] If the two parties desire amendment, Allah will make them of one mind.

Satan is a bad comrade, rebel, and one cursed by Allah. He misleads hypocrites and those who seek judgment from false deities far astray, though his strategy is weak. He claims an appointed portion of Allah’s bondmen, leads them astray, arouses desires in them, commands them to cut cattle’s ears and change Allah’s creation, and makes promises only to beguile.

l: the Last Day, Surah 4: The Women (An-Nisaa)
s: The Last Day is a day when people are accountable before Allah. Belief in it is presented as part of faith alongside belief in Allah, His angels, His Scriptures, and His messengers; rejecting these beliefs means wandering far astray. Believers are commanded to believe in the Last Day, including those directed to refer disputes to Allah and the messenger, and believers in Allah and the Last Day are promised immense reward. It is also linked with spending from what Allah has bestowed. On that day, those who disbelieved and disobeyed the messenger will wish they were level with the ground and will be unable to hide any fact from Allah.

Reward is a vast, immense benefit bestowed by Allah. An immense reward from Allah's presence is promised to those who do what they are exhorted to do. Allah promises good to both those who strive and those who remain behind, while granting the strivers a greater reward. For one who leaves home as a fugitive unto Allah and His messenger and dies before reaching the destination, the reward becomes incumbent on Allah. Believers who believe in Allah and His messengers without making distinction between them are to receive an immense reward and their wages from Allah.
A witness is brought from every people, and a witness is brought against these people. The unit does not identify the witnesses beyond this.

Scripture is something Allah reveals to Muhammad with the truth. It is given as a basis for judging between mankind, and Allah teaches Muhammad through it and wisdom what he did not know. It gives decrees, including concerning female orphans, marriage-related matters, weak children, and just treatment of orphans. It is also recited unto people and is an object of belief alongside the Scripture revealed aforetime. Those given a portion of it are criticized for purchasing error, seeking to make Muslims err, and changing words from their context; they are told to believe in what has been revealed confirming what they possess. Believers are directed not to sit where Allah's revelations are rejected and derided. Scripture thus unfolds from revelation and instruction, through judgment and decrees, to belief, justice, and warnings about rejection and distortion.

l: the right way, Surah 4: The Women (An-Nisaa)
s: Some people given a portion of the Scripture seek to make Muslims err from the right way.

The Jews are a group described through acts of disbelief, wrongdoing, and opposition to Allah’s way. Some change words from their context, distort religion with their tongues, speak words of disobedience, and slander religion. They break their covenant, disbelieve in Allah’s revelations, slay prophets wrongfully, speak against Mary with tremendous calumny, hinder Allah’s way, and are cursed by Allah for disbelief, though a few believe. Some given a portion of Scripture believe idols and false deities and regard idolaters as more rightly guided than believers. Their wrongdoing leads Allah to forbid them good things previously lawful. The account also highlights their taking usury despite prohibition and devouring people’s wealth by false pretences. It unfolds from their distortions and disbelief through covenant-breaking and grave accusations to divine cursing and the forbidding of lawful good things.

Disbelief is presented as a condition that brings Allah’s curse, blocks belief except for a few, and leads to punishment in the Fire for rejecting His revelations. Hypocrites are cast back into disbelief because of what they earned; they want believers to disbelieve as they do and become equal with them. The account culminates in a repeated pattern of believing, then disbelieving, then believing and disbelieving again, with increasing disbelief. Those who persist in that increase are neither pardoned by Allah nor guided to a way.

l: partners ascribed unto Allah, Surah 4: The Women (An-Nisaa)
s: Ascribing partners to Allah is presented as a tremendous sin and a grave error. It is not pardoned by Allah, except insofar as He wills, while other sins may be pardoned. The account first states that those who ascribe partners have invented a tremendous sin. It then reiterates that such ascription leads one far astray, contrasting this offense with wrongdoing Allah may otherwise forgive.

is_a deities [false] False deities are sought as judges by those who pretend to believe in what was revealed to the messenger and what was revealed before him. They had been ordered to abjure the false deities.

Abraham is an upright person whose house received from Allah the Scripture, wisdom, and a mighty kingdom. He is presented as surrendering his purpose to Allah while doing good and following the upright tradition. Most importantly, Allah chose Abraham as a friend. The records move from the blessings bestowed on his house to his personal devotion, goodness, upright way, and chosen friendship with Allah.

l: the house of Abraham, Surah 4: The Women (An-Nisaa)
s: The house of Abraham is a group that received Scripture, wisdom, and a mighty kingdom from Allah. It is presented through a passage addressing believers’ conduct in prayer and purification, then promising Gardens, pure companions, and shade to those who believe and do good works; within this setting, Allah bestows these gifts on the house of Abraham.

Hell is a place of burning, habitation, and final destination for those marked by disbelief, wrongdoing, opposition after guidance, following other than the believer’s way, choosing Satan instead of Allah, and hypocrisy. It is sufficient as burning for those who turn away from what was given to them. It is called an evil and hapless journey’s end, particularly for those taken in death while wronging themselves and failing to migrate despite having the ability. Those who choose Satan instead of Allah will inhabit it and find no refuge. Allah will gather hypocrites and disbelievers there together. Those who disbelieve and deal in wrong will abide in Hell forever.

l: the revelations of Allah, Surah 4: The Women (An-Nisaa)
s: Allah’s revelations are disbelieved, rejected, and derided by disbelievers.
